features.t: Virtual networks (create, get, list, delete) over ARM

x: Only IPv4 CIDR prefixes are modelled; IPv6 address spaces are not.

Name, address range, the private-subnet (defaultOutboundAccess) flag, NSG, route table and NAT gateway associations are real and drive behaviour (system routes incl. None for RFC1918 outside the vnet, UDRs, NAT/default outbound egress). The console's Add subnet dialog's NAT gateway and Route table pickers select from real Microsoft.Network/natGateways and routeTables (created over ARM/CLI; this lens has no dedicated console for either yet, same as NSGs' earlier state). NIC private IPs are allocated from the subnet (.0-.3 and the last address reserved). Subnet delegation is not modelled.

Adding a peering creates the real ARM peering object on both virtual networks (same as the portal's Add blade), with peeringState fixed at 'Connected' and peeringSyncLevel fixed at 'FullyInSync' — Vyomi has no asynchronous sync process to model, so 'Sync' is a no-op refresh.
A service endpoint is stored as a {service, locations} entry on the subnet, same as real ARM. Service endpoint policies (restricting which resource instances are reachable) are not modelled.

features.t: Resource locks (Microsoft.Authorization/locks), scoped to this virtual network
x: Lock create/list/delete are real Microsoft.Authorization/locks over ARM at resource, resource-group and subscription scope (CanNotDelete/ReadOnly, name and notes validated); this blade manages the locks scoped to this virtual network only and has no scope switch. A resource-group or subscription lock really blocks writes and deletes of everything under it with 409 ScopeLocked (core/azure_arm_ext_core.py lock_conflict), but a lock set directly on a virtual network is stored and listed only: it does not block writes or deletes of the virtual network itself.

Only console/SDK-triggered mutations made since the simulation booted are recorded (no historical backfill); severity/category filtering and the 7/30/90-day timespan picker are not modelled, and `caller` is a fixed placeholder identity rather than the real signed-in principal.
The ARM Template, Bicep and Terraform tabs are all generated client-side from this resource's live ARM state; linked/nested templates and deployment history are not modelled.

Role assignments and role definitions are real ARM resources (Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments, roleDefinitions), and Check access / My access run the real wildcard + scope-inheritance + notActions + explicit-deny decision — all ENFORCED scoped to this virtual network (plus its subscription/resource-group ancestors, matching real Azure's inherited-access view); Roles stays subscription-wide, which matches real Azure (built-in role definitions are listed tenant-wide too). Deny assignments and Classic administrators remain an honest gap — Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management and the legacy Azure Service Management administrator list are not modelled. Update: the Deny assignments list, Classic administrators (a read-only list of the subscription's account administrator, like the real API) and My access (the simulated signed-in principal, evaluated with checkAccess) are now real shared tabs (azure.common.*); the gap wording above predates them.

features.t: Diagnose and solve problems (remaining tiles), Resource visualizer, Tasks, Support + Troubleshooting
x: Resource visualizer is real — the same ARM reads the Subnets/Connected devices/Peerings panels use, grouped into cards per subnet — rendered as cards rather than Azure's interactive canvas diagram. Tasks (preview) is built as a browser-local (localStorage) per-resource task list: real Azure's Tasks feature isn't a documented ARM resource provider Vyomi can model natively, and it's the same kind of console-local bookkeeping as 'Pin to dashboard'. Support + Troubleshooting is a real navigational hub (links to Diagnose and solve problems, a static 'Available' resource-health readout) except filing an actual support ticket, which needs Microsoft's own support ticketing service. Diagnose and solve problems' IP flow verify, Next hop and Connection troubleshoot tiles are real — see azure.vnets.network_watcher — but its remaining diagnostic tiles stay an honest gap: they run Azure's AI-driven troubleshooting recommendations (VPN/ExpressRoute/DNS) against Microsoft's own analytics backend, not a deterministic local ARM read.

features.t: Diagnose and solve problems / Monitoring: IP flow verify, Next hop, Connection troubleshoot (Network Watcher)
x: IP flow verify, Next hop and Connection troubleshoot all answer from the shared netsim evaluator (core/netsim) — the same engine behind AWS Reachability Analyzer and GCP Connectivity Tests — scoped to a virtual machine's network interface in this virtual network's subnets. Vyomi auto-provisions the regional NetworkWatcher_<location> resource the first time any of the three tools runs in a location, same as the real portal's 'Enable Network Watcher' behaviour. Connection troubleshoot's hop-by-hop trace uses Vyomi's own component labels (route-table/nsg/peering/...), not real Network Watcher's hop-type enum, and offers TCP/UDP (this evaluator's protocols) rather than real Azure's TCP/ICMP. There is no standalone Network Watcher service console yet, only these diagnostic tools reached from the NSG and Virtual network blades.

features.t: Topology (subnets, their connected devices, and peered virtual networks)
x: The data is real — the same ARM reads the Subnets, Connected devices and Peerings panels use (subnet address ranges, NSG/route table/NAT gateway associations, attached network interfaces, peering state) — but it is rendered as a structured list rather than Azure's interactive canvas diagram.

Diagnostic settings is real — the same Microsoft.Insights/diagnosticSettings extension-resource mechanism the NSG lens wires (core/azure_monitor_core.py); logs/metrics are stored and validated exactly as the real resource requires, but — same as every other resource in this lens — never delivered anywhere. Logs runs real KQL (core/azure_operationalinsights_core.py's small supported subset: where/project/sort by/take/count) against a chosen Log Analytics workspace's real AzureActivity table, the SAME rows this vnet's own Activity log tab reads; every other table is always empty (no agent/telemetry ingestion pipeline). Alerts lists real Microsoft.Insights/metricAlerts and activityLogAlerts rules whose own 'scopes' names this vnet (the generic alert-rule resources the Monitor service's Alerts page lists subscription-wide) — Vyomi stores alert rules but runs no live metric-evaluation loop, so none has ever fired, same honest limitation as azure.monitor.alert_rules. Metrics: Microsoft.Network/virtualNetworks publishes no real-time telemetry Vyomi can emulate (core/azure_monitor_core.py: 'Not modelled: metric definitions / metrics'), so instead of a stored/random chart this tile shows a REAL derived series — this vnet's own management-operation count per hour, read back from its Activity log — never synthetic data; it is a Vyomi-native substitute for the real ARM metric catalog, not that catalog itself.

Microsoft.Network/networkManagers with networkGroups (+ staticMembers), connectivityConfigurations (Mesh / HubAndSpoke) and securityAdminConfigurations (ruleCollections + rules) are real ARM resources: scope accesses gate which configuration kinds are allowed, target groups and hub/member vnets must exist, rule priorities (1-4096) and ports are validated, and a group/vnet/manager in use cannot be deleted. There is no commit/deploy step and nothing is applied to the network: no peerings are created from a connectivity configuration and security admin rules are not evaluated against traffic.

Microsoft.Network/privateEndpoints is a real ARM resource: the subnet and target resource must exist, groupIds are validated per target type, a private IP is allocated from the subnet (never .0-.3), customDnsConfigs carry the privatelink FQDN, and a privateEndpointConnections child is written on the target (auto-Approved, or Pending for manual connections) where approve/reject/delete flow back to the endpoint. No packet is routed: the endpoint does not change how the target's own data plane is reached, publicNetworkAccess=Disabled is not enforced against traffic, and private DNS zone groups are not created. Targets: storage, Key Vault, SQL, Cosmos DB, Container Registry, Redis; App Configuration and Cognitive Services connections are mirrored onto the target resource's own privateEndpointConnections list and approve/reject/delete there flows back to the endpoint.

Bastion hosts are real ARM resources with real validation (AzureBastionSubnet name and /26 minimum, Standard static public IP, SKU-gated features and instance counts). There is no guest network stack to tunnel to, so Connect sessions (browser RDP/SSH, native client) are not available.

Azure Firewall and firewall policies are real ARM resources (AzureFirewallSubnet /26, Standard static public IP, tier must match the policy, Basic requires a management subnet + IP, rule collection / group priorities 100-65000 and unique, a private IP is allocated from the subnet; policies in use cannot be deleted). The rule base is EVALUATED on both substrates through the simulator action POST .../azureFirewalls/{fw}/evaluate (core/azure_firewall_eval.py): DNAT, then network, then application rules, each by rule-collection-group then rule-collection priority, base-policy rules first, implicit deny, IP/CIDR/range/FQDN (leading wildcard) and port-range matching, and the DNAT translation is reported. Not modelled: the firewall is not inserted into UDR/netsim routing (no VM traffic is filtered), threat-intelligence deny, IDPS, TLS inspection, IP Groups / FQDN tags / web categories (rules using them are skipped and reported), SNAT; the Rules / Threat intelligence / IDPS authoring screens are not built.

DDoS protection plans are real ARM resources; attaching a plan to a vnet is validated and tracked (the plan lists its protected vnets, an in-use plan cannot be deleted). No attack mitigation or telemetry exists: nothing is ever scrubbed, and DDoS metrics/alerts are not produced.

The list is a real ARM read (every Microsoft.Network/networkInterfaces resource in the subscription whose ipConfigurations[].subnet.id points at one of this vnet's subnets), so a NIC attached via ARM/the CLI/another tool shows up here. Device Type is always reported as 'Network interface' — Vyomi has no DHCP lease / ARP table to discover non-NIC clients (VMs/devices that never registered a network interface resource).

features.t: IP address pools (Allocate using IP address pools) and advertised address prefixes (BGP)
x: IP address pools are real: Microsoft.Network/networkManagers/{nm}/ipamPools is a genuine nested ARM resource (core/azure_arm_data.py CATALOG, reached through the generic type/name alternation — no dedicated code, same mechanic as a container registry's webhooks), and the Create VNet wizard's 'Allocate using IP address pools' checkbox ENFORCES a real, non-overlapping CIDR block carved out of the chosen pool's own address space (AzureArm._allocate_ipam_pool) — never a stored label; the block is released back to the pool when its vnet is deleted. Per-subnet pool allocation is not modelled: a pool-allocated vnet always gets one 'default' subnet spanning its full allocated range. Advertised address prefixes (custom BGP route advertisement) are not modelled: they only affect routing once this vnet peers with a real ExpressRoute circuit's carrier-network routers — hardware outside anything a local simulator can model — so Vyomi stores no advertised gateway prefixes.

features.t: Subnet service endpoints and delegation (create-subnet dialog)
x: Service endpoints are validated against the supported list and are what the data planes really check: a virtual network rule on Storage, Cosmos DB, Service Bus, Azure AI services and SQL is accepted by ARM only for a subnet that carries the matching endpoint (SubnetsHaveNoServiceEndpointsConfigured otherwise), and a declared caller in that subnet passes the firewall only with both the rule and the endpoint. Delegations are validated (known services, no duplicates, not on a subnet with a private endpoint).

advertisedAddressPrefixes are validated (CIDRs, within the address space, no duplicates) and round-trip on the virtual network. Custom BGP advertisement only matters once the network peers with a gateway/ExpressRoute circuit, which does not exist in a local simulator, so nothing is advertised.

Control plane only: profiles (AFD Standard/Premium + classic CDN SKUs, SKU change rules), afdEndpoints (derived *.z01.azurefd.net host), originGroups + origins (health probe / load balancing / priority / weight / port ranges), routes (origin group, rule set and custom domain cross references, pattern/protocol validation, conflict detection), ruleSets + rules (condition/action names, unique order) and customDomains (managed/customer TLS, Pending DNS validation token), with in-use delete protection. No edge request is ever served: no caching, WAF, TLS termination, or origin health probing, and custom domains never leave Pending. The console has a Front Door and CDN profiles service (#/frontdoor: profiles, endpoints, origin groups + origins, routes, rule sets + rules, custom domains) and a Network managers service (#/networkmanagers: groups, security admin configurations -> rule collections -> admin rules, connectivity configurations) over these same ARM resources; there is no Deploy step, so security admin rules are never evaluated against traffic.

features.t: Virtual Network Manager: deploy connectivity configurations and evaluate security admin rules
x: Deploy is real for Connectivity: Mesh and HubAndSpoke commits write peerings into the member virtual networks (visible to the VNet Peerings blade, Network Watcher next hop and the netsim engine); each commit replaces the peerings the manager created before. SecurityAdmin commits activate the rules for the on-demand Effective rules evaluation (priority order across collections; Deny beats NSG allow, AlwaysAllow bypasses NSGs). Only static group members (no Azure Policy conditional membership), no routing configurations, and Deny/AlwaysAllow verdicts are not yet consumed by the Docker/nftables data path for live packets.
